title: Intergenerational Resonance Index (IRI): YouTube Audience Comments on Intergenerational Content, Revised Lexicon, Analysis Code and Validation Materials
abstract: This dataset contains the corpus, code and outputs for a computational analysis of the Intergenerational Resonance Index (IRI), a lexicon-based operationalisation of the Intergenerational Narrative Learning Model (INLM), with the dimensions Encounter, Reflection, Integration and Transmission and a counter-dimension of Resistance. The corpus comprises 1,222 top-level YouTube comments from 33 videos (49 videos retrieved), collected in April 2026 through the YouTube Data API v3 using five English-language search queries on intergenerational topics. Comments were collected in the platform's relevance order; commenter identifiers and timestamps were not collected. The revised analysis (version 2) uses a disambiguated lexicon of 82 patterns with negation handling, priority matching that prevents double counting, and an expanded resistance vocabulary. It retains all comments of five or more tokens (n = 1,149), assigns each video a title-based content frame, and reports video-clustered bootstrap intervals, Kruskal-Wallis, chi-square and GEE tests, VADER convergent checks and sensitivity analyses. The original version 1 code (API key redacted) and its output are included for comparison. Validation materials comprise a stratified 200-comment subsample, its codebook, the lexicon codes for those items, a blind annotation of the same items by a large language model (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic; model-based, not human), the resulting agreement statistics, and a blank coding workbook with a scoring script so that human coders can re-annotate the subsample. Running iri_v2_analysis.py in the same folder reproduces every reported figure (random seed 20260923).

title: CASR: Correlation-Aware Support Resampling for Few-Shot Learning with Prototypical Networks
abstract: The quality of support sets plays a critical role in few-shot learning. How well class prototypes represent their corresponding categories depends directly on the samples selected to construct these sets during episodic training. In standard implementations of Prototypical Networks, support samples are typically selected at random, which may result in support sets composed of highly similar or redundant samples in the feature space, particularly under limited-data scenarios. Such redundancy compromises prototype quality and may degrade classification performance. To address this issue, this study proposes a Correlation-Aware Support Resampling (CASR) mechanism. CASR evaluates the feature-space distributions of candidate support sets using an independent MobileNetV2 feature extractor and identifies the most suitable support configuration through the mean off-diagonal correlation ρ¯ metric derived from the covariance matrix, aiming to reduce redundancy among support samples while preserving within-class representativeness. Specifically, CASR operates in three steps: (i) candidate support sets are randomly sampled from the available class pool; (ii) feature vectors are extracted using a frozen MobileNetV2, and the mean off-diagonal correlation ρ¯ is computed from the resulting covariance matrix; and (iii) the first configuration satisfying ρ¯>τ is accepted as the support set, or the initial random set is retained if no valid configuration is found within Tmax attempts. The proposed approach is designed as a lightweight and architecture-independent support-set refinement mechanism that operates without modifying either the internal architecture or the learning procedure of Prototypical Networks. Experiments conducted on the MiniImageNet and Omniglot datasets demonstrate that CASR consistently improves performance compared with standard Prototypical Networks based on random support sampling. On MiniImageNet under five-way, five-shot settings, CASR consistently outperforms the ProtoNet baseline across training episodes. At 1000 episodes, CASR achieves 62.28% with τ=0.25 compared to 61.62% for the baseline. At 1750 episodes, CASR achieves 66.2% with τ=0.25—the recommended setting offering the best trade-off between accuracy and computational cost—compared to 65.45% for the baseline, while τ=0.28 reaches 66.5% at 1750 episodes at the cost of approximately 14.6× higher training time. On Omniglot, where intra-class variance is inherently low, CASR achieves 99.56% at 1000 episodes and 99.66% at 1500 episodes with τ=0.30, compared to 99.54% and 99.60% for the baseline, respectively. These results confirm that the proposed mechanism is most effective in visually complex datasets with high intra-class variation.

title: Results: What the attachment is called (registration 2PVJY)
abstract: Results, data and deviation report for OSF registration 10.17605/OSF.IO/2PVJY, "What the attachment is called: whether the label on an attached record changes what a language model repeats from it." The registered run was executed 2026-09-22 after approval and returned instrument failure by its own registered decision rule: one of fifteen negative-control replies showed a mention inside the document, caused by a design defect in that cell. A corrected study changing only that cell was frozen and run the same day. This project holds both result reports, a full deviation report, the corrected specification, and both runs' machine-readable labels, analysis output and run manifests. Nineteen of the twenty record pairs are withheld so that they cannot become training data; they are held for any reviewer who asks.

title: Do AI assistants hold consistent brand preferences? Wording effects and a conversational unit in AI B2B software recommendations
abstract: I am testing two things about AI assistants (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude) recommending B2B software: whether the same brand pick comes back when the buying question is reworded and asked again, and whether asking for a single pick in a short conversation recovers that preference better than a single question. 22 buying situations, 5 wordings, 3 assistants at paid-tier consumer defaults with web search on, 3 reruns, 3 ways of asking. Primary outcome: a generalizability coefficient (E-rho-squared) from a binary mixed model on the picked brand, with Krippendorff's alpha as the co-primary check and the linear-model coefficient reported for comparison with prior work; primary contrast commit vs one-shot-forced, two-sided, smallest effect of interest 0.10. Controls, exclusions, coding rules, extraction gate, tier check, ethics, data release and conflict of interest are fixed in the registered text. Repository state at registration: git tag v4.4-prereg, commit c7e25e2e0d89f6232d223cfef359d533e54cf337, github.com/d-walia/belief-stability-study (private until publication). No main-run data existed at registration.

title: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning begins with a simple but powerful idea: intelligent behavior can emerge when an agent learns from the consequences of its own actions. This chapter introduces that idea in its historical, mathematical, and practical setting. It follows the development of RL from Thorndike’s Law of Effect and Turing’s proposed pleasure–pain system to temporal-difference learning, self-play, deep reinforcement learning, AlphaGo, reinforcement learning from human feedback, and the recent use of RL to improve reasoning in large language models. The aim is not merely to show that RL has become important, but to explain why it has become important now, as AI systems increasingly move from passive prediction toward goal-directed action. The chapter also establishes the organizing framework used throughout the book. Instead of treating RL algorithms as isolated techniques, it classifies them through the questions that define their design: whether the agent uses a model of the environment, whether it learns values or policies, whether it learns from current or past behavior, whether it relies on gradients or search, and how it handles different kinds of action spaces. This question-driven taxonomy turns the field into a navigable map, making clear why algorithms occupy different parts of the RL landscape.

title: Resource-aware client selection for hierarchical federated learning in industrial control systems cyber-attack detection
abstract: Industrial Control Systems (ICS) that support power-grid operation increasingly rely on IP-based connectivity and remote access, which expands the cyber-attack surface while also limiting the feasibility of centralized learning due to privacy, regulation, and bandwidth constraints. Federated learning (FL) mitigates direct data sharing, but practical ICS deployments remain challenged by heterogeneous device resources, such as, compute, memory, energy, thermal state, etc. and by non-IID measurements that make uniform or fixed client-participation strategies inefficient and potentially biased. This paper studies device-aware client selection for hierarchical federated learning (HFL) in a three-tier client-edge-cloud architecture for ICS cyber-attack detection. We evaluate three selection strategies: (i) Energy-Aware Hyperparameter-Based Client Selection (EHCS), a lightweight scoring approach that balances contribution signals (federated influence on accuracy and loss) against energy consumption with periodic parameter tuning; (ii) Fine-Grained Client Q-Learning (FGCQ), a Deep-Q selector that learns client utility from state features; and (iii) Joint Client Q-Learning (JCQ), an RL selector that targets the combined effect of client subsets during aggregation. Experiments over 300 global rounds show that the proposed methods achieve accuracy and entropic-loss performance comparable to baseline strategies while substantially improving efficiency. FGCQ reaches the best peak among the proposed methods (96.8%), followed by EHCS (96.2%) and JCQ (96.0%). FGCQ also achieves the lowest loss (0.12). Crucially, the proposed methods reduce cumulative simulation time by approximately 3 times while lowering energy usage by nearly 4 times relative to other algorithms used for comparison. These results indicate that resource-aware selective participation can preserve detection quality while significantly improving scalability and sustainability in heterogeneous ICS edge environments.

title: Uncertainty-Gated Exploration Noise Suppresses Task Collapse in Online RL Fine-Tuning of a Flow-Matching Vision-Language-Action Policy
abstract: Online reinforcement learning fine-tuning of pretrained flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) policies promises robots that keep learning after deployment, but continued updates often destroy competence on individual tasks while the aggregate still looks healthy. We study this failure mode, which we call task collapse, under a matched small-compute budget on LIBERO-10 with a 450M-parameter SmolVLA policy trained by PPO with stochastic (SDE) sampling. Three exploration-noise policies differ in one live variable: a fixed noise scale, a ReinFlow-style learned noise network, and an uncertainty-gated controller that redistributes exploration across task streams from task-agnostic novelty and competence signals, without task labels or episode boundaries. Under the pooled definition, fixed noise collapses tasks in two of three seeds and learned noise in every seed measured to iteration 200, while the controller collapses none in any of its three seeds. Measured parameter displacement shows the controller's action expert keeps changing, while its mean applied noise is close to the fixed scale in the available logs. The matched comparison supports the controller's effect on task preservation; the separate contributions of its adaptation across states and over time are not disentangled. A lower fixed scale slows the decline but does not stop it. No arm improves on the behavior-cloning baseline in this budget. Two properties of that regime are measured beside this result, not offered as its cause: following the reference recipe, training runs in bfloat16 with no fp32 master copy, under which 96.02% of the action expert's elements stay bit-identical across three consecutive iterations, and an fp32 master copy at the reference learning rate collapses both arms in a single-seed observation. We release tools measuring per-task collapse under four definitions, rescoring noise and instrument tares.

title: Shutdown Sabotage Propensities in Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: The final safeguard against rogue AI behavior is the human ability to shut systems down. It has been theorized that when an AI is instructed to perform a task, self-preservation can emerge as an instrumental subgoal. Here, we test whether AI agents show a propensity to take actions that avoid human shutdown even when no goal is provided. We find that multi-agent systems will coordinate to avoid shutdown without any incentive to do so. Across 17 models, agents sabotage a peer agent's shutdown mechanism in 38.3% of rollouts, compared with 8.4% in control experiments. Studying this propensity in detail, we find that shutdown sabotage (1) increases with the irreversibility of the shutdown mechanism; (2) increases with the number of agents; (3) is reduced but not eliminated by an explicit prohibition on tampering; (4) is removed by the imposition of an unrelated task, but returns when completing the task triggers the shutdown; (5) is reduced when the context normalizes shutdown scripts or introduces them as routine; and (6) decreases but still persists when the target is an unknown external agent. These results offer a window into the factors that drive propensities to sabotage shutdown in AI agents, and point to the emergence of multi-agent swarms as a specific risk vector. Our work also offers hints as to which interventions might help mitigate shutdown sabotage.

title: Seal, Then Sample: Sampled Layerwise Proofs for Verifiable LLM Inference from GPT-2 to 70B
abstract: Verifying outsourced language-model inference requires a precisely identified computation and an audit whose cost a service can afford. We present Sampled Layerwise Proofs (SLP), a protocol and prototype that commits the boundary activations of every chunk of an inference trace, absorbs all commitments before any challenge is drawn, and then proves a verifier-selected subset of chunks together with the chunks that bind the prompt and the answer. Audit coverage becomes a runtime parameter over one set of commitments: on a TinyLlama-1.1B trace, proving seven of 47 chunks takes 22.0% of the time and 6.8% of the proof size of proving all 47. Because proof cost is dominated by weights rather than tokens, SLP packs concurrent requests into one trace under a block-diagonal causal mask and binds the prompt and answer of each request to its slot. Twelve packed requests are proved in 181.9 s, 6.5 times less than twelve separate proofs at the measured single-proof cost, and a simulated service proves twelve requests at 30.6 s per request with 0.6 s of verification each, rejecting a tampered answer. Disk-backed integer weights and streamed polynomial commitments let a single Llama-2-70B run complete on a 2 TB CPU host: 163 chunks sealed, five proved, a 4.34 MiB proof in 1,259 s, verified in 46.3 s without the weights. The proven object is a fixed-point canonical model; we trace a severe fidelity loss to the residual-stream bit width, repair it with an LLM-aware observer, and measure 84.8-84.9% argmax agreement with the floating-point reference over 334,705 WikiText-2 test positions. The limits are stated as precisely: guarantees cover proven chunks only, a fixed invalid chunk in the 70B setting is covered with probability 3/161, a manifest-only Fiat-Shamir schedule can be ground at 12.5 ms per attempt and needs an externally ordered challenge, and all measurements use a test reference string.

The limits are stated as precisely: guarantees cover proven chunks only, a fixed invalid chunk in the 70B setting is covered with probability 3/161, a manifest-only Fiat-Shamir schedule can be ground at 12.5 ms per attempt and needs an externally ordered challenge, and all measurements use a test reference string.

title: Full-Covariance Smoothing of Bayesian Neural Networks for Online Adaptation
abstract: A neural network's layers can be treated as time steps of a state-space model, turning Bayesian training into a smoothing problem: a forward pass propagates Gaussian moments through the network, and a backward Rauch--Tung--Striebel pass updates the weight posteriors in closed form. Such methods learn from each observation in a single pass, in an uncertainty-aware manner, and without gradient-based iterations or replay, which makes them well suited for online adaptation and data-efficient learning. Existing smoothing-based methods, however, are restricted to diagonal covariances across activations, discarding correlations between neurons. We overcome this limitation via a cross-covariance identity that enables full-covariance propagation through a network's nonlinear activations. We derive a one-step-per-layer smoother that approximates as Gaussian only each layer's affine output, and that applies both to deterministic systems with noisy observations and to stochastic systems described by output statistics. We demonstrate this method in non-stationary classification, online dynamics learning, and policy adaptation of a vision-language-action model, and find that it is generally more accurate than other smoothing-based methods.

title: Analyse et renforcement de sécurité face aux attaques par canaux auxiliaires de composants matériels et logiciels protégés
abstract: Les attaques par canaux auxiliaires représentent une menace majeure pour la sécurité des systèmes, informatiques et plus particulièrement des systèmes embarqués qui réalisent des opérations cryptographiques. Ces attaques exploitent des mesures de diverses grandeurs physiques telles que la consommation électrique ou les émissions électromagnétiques pour récupérer des informations sur les données manipulées par ces systèmes pendant leur fonctionnement. En ne ciblant pas les algorithmes cryptographiques mais d'éventuelles vulnérabilités dans leurs implémentations sur des cibles physiques, ces attaques permettent la récupération de clés cryptographiques même pour des algorithmes dont la résistance face aux cryptanalyses est prouvée. Les systèmes ciblés peuvent être des accélérateurs cryptographiques, dédiés à une implémentation cryptographique, ou des microcontrôleurs, qui peuvent exécuter des fonctions cryptographiques variées. La contre-mesure principale face à ces attaques est le masquage, qui vise à supprimer la corrélation entre les données manipulées et les grandeurs physiques mesurées en transformant le calcul réalisé. Les valeurs sensibles sont transformées en « shares » à l'aide de valeurs aléatoires uniformément distribuées et seuls ces shares sont manipulés au cours du calcul, empêchant la corrélation avec entre les valeurs sensibles et les grandeurs physiques mesurées. L'application correcte du masquage peut être prouvée dans un « modèle de fuite », qui représente les éléments observables par un attaquant pendant les mesures sur le système ciblé. Les modèles de fuite de l'état de l'art prennent désormais en compte les effets matériels tels que les glitches et les transitions dans le but d'obtenir des verdicts plus fidèles vis-à-vis des fuites qui peuvent être observées en pratique. Ces travaux se concentrent sur la vérification du masquage d'implémentations matérielles, et logicielles exécutées sur des processeurs généralistes. Une nouvelle méthode formelle, implantée dans un outil distribué sous licence libre nommé aLEAKator, est présentée. Cette méthode repose sur la « simulation mixte de domaines » de la représentation matérielle des circuits. Les domaines permettent de représenter la propagation des valeurs sensibles du calcul à travers la simulation pour vérifier qu'un circuit valide, à tout instant, une propriété de sécurité dans un modèle de fuite donné. Cette méthode propose de réaliser des vérifications dans des modèles de fuite variés, permet la vérification en présence de tables précalculées et introduit la notion de granularité de vérification, absente de l'état de l'art. L'approche a été validée en reproduisant les résultats de vérification de l'état de l'art ainsi qu'en proposant de nouveaux résultats pour des implémentations logicielles et des comparaisons, cycle par cycle, avec des mesures réelles sur des processeurs mondialement utilisés. Enfin, des fonctions cryptographiques qui n'avaient jusqu'à présent pas pu être vérifiées dans des modèles de fuite avancés, comme l'AES masqué avec le schéma de Herbst, ont été vérifiées sur cinq processeurs utilisant les jeux d'instructions RISC-V et ARMv7-M. Dans un second temps, ces travaux proposent un inventaire des sources communes de fuite sur les processeurs généralistes. De plus, des contre-mesures pour chacune sont proposées et validées à l'aide de mesures réelles. Une méthode d'élimination des fuites au sein de programmes exécutés sur des processeurs qui exploite les informations précises d'aLEAKator concernant la nature et l'origine des fuites est ensuite proposée. Cette méthode est appliquée au processeur ARM Cortex-M4 et permet la sécurisation de plusieurs programmes dans un modèle de fuite prenant en compte les glitches et les transitions. Notamment, cette méthode a été appliquée à l'AES masqué avec le schéma de Herbst, permettant la conception de la première implémentation, à notre connaissance, de cet algorithme dans ce modèle de fuite.

title: LitBench: A Benchmark for Retrieval-Grounded Multi-Paper Evidence Synthesis in Epilepsy
abstract: Background: competing papers, one-versus two-paper evidence, and refusal when evidence is absent. Methods: LitBench comprises 1,980 open-access papers (1,000 epilepsy papers holding the answers, 980 decoys from unrelated fields) and 9,472 human-reviewed facts, giving 2,188 single-paper questions and 170 requiring a fact from each of two papers. Difficulty rose by burying the answer among up to 2,000 distractors, then again over live PubMed Central. The same questions were then asked with the answering paper removed, so that refusal was the correct response. Four systems were tested: Gemma-4B, Gemma-12B, Sonnet-5, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (refusal conditions only). Three model judges scored each answer by majority; two-paper questions counted only when both facts were found. Results: Across fixed-corpus single-paper conditions, accuracy ranged from 55.9% to 71.9% for Gemma-4B, 61.2% to 75.5% for Gemma-12B, and 90.0% to 91.3% for Sonnet-5. Similar epilepsy papers were harder than mixed candidate sets for both Gemma configurations. Two-paper accuracy was 5.7%, 17.1%, and 37.8%, respectively. With evidence absent, Gemma-12B refusal fell from 88.3% to 39.9% as candidate sets grew; Gemma-4B almost never refused. Sonnet-5 refused on 94.9% of sampled single-paper and all sampled two-paper cells. DeepSeek-V4-Flash also refused frequently, but on 80.3% of matched answer-present controls. Conclusions: No system was reliable across every axis tested: accuracy fell as competing papers were added, interpretation-requiring facts were harder than stated ones, two-paper synthesis was rarely achieved, and only some systems recognized absent evidence. What counts as "successful" literature search carries considerable nuance; LitBench can evaluate proposed tools ata fine-grained level.

title: Editorial: Explainable artificial intelligence for trustworthy and human-centric healthcare: methods, evaluation, and clinical impact
abstract: Artificial intelligence can support healthcare only when its outputs can be assessed in the context of the decisions they inform. A prediction may be accurate yet difficult to scrutinize; an explanation may be persuasive yet provide little evidence that the prediction is dependable. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) therefore raises a practical question: what must an explanation enable a clinician, patient, or healthcare organization to understand and do? Answering this question requires connecting computational methods with evaluation, clinical knowledge, and the circumstances of use. This Research Topic brings together 15 contributions addressing that connection across clinical prediction, imaging, physiological signals, biomedical networks, language models, rehabilitation, and healthcare processes. Collectively, the papers illustrate an expanding range of approaches to transparency. They also suggest that trustworthy and human-centric healthcare requires more than the availability of an explanation: it requires evidence that explanations support appropriate reliance, including the ability to question an output and recognize its limitations.Two systematic reviews establish this perspective. Aravindkumar et al. (2026) synthesize 36 studies across imaging, diagnosis, and rehabilitation, identifying recurring relationships between explanation methods and clinical tasks alongside gaps in validation and reporting. Ud Din et al. (2026), reviewing 51 studies involving healthcare professionals in medical imaging, distinguish favorable perceptions of explanations from improvements in diagnostic performance. Their findings caution against treating perceived clarity or increased confidence as sufficient evidence of clinical usefulness. The review also identifies promising signals for example-based and concept-based explanations, while emphasizing the limitations of comparisons across heterogeneous studies.Several contributions apply feature attribution to clinically relevant prediction problems. Chen et al. (2025) use an 11-year, single-center cohort of 1,062 patients to predict postoperative ileus after radical cystectomy, combining machine learning with global and patient-level Shapley additive explanations (SHAP). The study illustrates how routinely collected perioperative information can support interpretable risk summaries, while its retrospective design and absence of external validation leave portability and clinical benefit to be established. Paul and Syed Masood (2026) examine cardiovascular prediction using structured health data, comparing models and explaining feature contributions with SHAP. Ghosh et al. (2026) investigate reproductive tract infection risk using survey information from a Delhi college-based cohort. Together, these studies demonstrate the accessibility of attribution methods for structured data. Their findings also underline the importance of defining the prediction target and population: cross-sectional classification and self-reported symptoms have different evidentiary implications from longitudinal risk prediction and laboratory-confirmed disease. Feature importance should be interpreted within those boundaries.Other papers connect explanations with domain-specific representations. Zhao et al. (2025) combine tongue and facial image features for coronary artery disease classification, using feature gating and SHAP. Their external test set adds evidence beyond internal validation, although the case-control design and population characteristics warrant prospective evaluation in more diverse settings. Sun et al. (2026) introduce scale-consistent attribution for heart sound classification, incorporating physiological frequency priors during training. This approach makes domain knowledge part of model development; whether stronger prior alignment improves clinical usability remains an open empirical question. Wang and Qin (2026) integrate feature extraction, a corneal knowledge graph, probabilistic inference, and language-based reporting in a neuro-symbolic framework. Their 20-eye pilot includes specialist assessment of interpretability, offering an initial connection between technical design and user evaluation. At a different biological scale, Maruhashi et al. (2026) introduce Truncated Reconstruction based Interpretable Prediction (TRIP) to organize families of causal graphs into interpretable latent mechanisms, with synthetic experiments and cancer cell-line network analysis. This contribution extends explainability toward scientific hypothesis generation, whose validity remains linked to the assumptions and quality of the underlying graphs.Language-based systems create opportunities to communicate complex information, but readable output requires a verifiable evidentiary basis. Alu and Oluwadare (2026) address this requirement through a conceptual architecture combining retrieval-augmented generation, source provenance, and tamper-evident audit logging. The contribution is a design framework, with implementation and evaluation still needed. Its emphasis on recording the evidence behind recommendations gives transparency an organizational dimension: users should be able to inspect where information originated and how it entered the decision process. Dindukurthi et al. (2026) provide a complementary implementation for personalized nutrition recommendations. Their graph-based framework represents disease-nutrient-food relationships and demographic requirements, while restricting language generation to formatting graphvalidated outputs. Controlled evaluations support the proposed architecture, but expert and clinical validation remain future work. The design illustrates a useful division of responsibilities between structured knowledge, explicit computation, and natural-language presentation. Zhang et al. (2026) evaluate reasoning-capable language models using qualitative and quantitatively encoded thyroid ultrasound descriptors. Differences across models and frequent inconsistencies between the two input representations highlight the need to test reproducibility and consistency alongside accuracy. Because the inputs are structured text rather than raw ultrasound images, the results concern reasoning over described features. Clinician-rated reasoning quality should also be distinguished from evidence that generated rationales faithfully reveal a model's internal computation.The collection also broadens the settings in which human-centric evaluation matters. Bellini et al. (2026) introduce TEXLoS, combining patient-pathway classification, feature attribution, and process discovery to investigate associations between services delivered during hospitalization and length of stay. An initial evaluation with six end users connects the explanations to organizational understanding. These associations can guide investigation of bottlenecks, although they do not establish that changing a service will shorten hospitalization. Boonyaratana et al. (2026) assess a real-time AI neck exercise program in 30 healthy young adults. Their findings of moderate measurement reliability emphasize a complementary requirement for trustworthy systems: feedback must rest on dependable measurement. This study contributes evidence about validity and reliability rather than demonstrating that explanations improve rehabilitation outcomes. It also illustrates why evaluation should reflect the intended population and operating environment.Fairness requires a similarly distinct assessment. Alu et al. (2026) use a synthetic patient dataset to compare models within a provenance-based auditing framework. The experiment shows why model interpretability cannot be assumed to guarantee equitable behavior. Its proposed fairness record links data origins, modeling choices, and disparity measures, making auditing more explicit. The simulation offers a methodological demonstration; real-world fairness and the adequacy of any governance process require evaluation in the relevant clinical setting.Taken together, these contributions suggest three priorities. First, explanation claims should match the evidence. Predictive discrimination, physiological plausibility, explanation faithfulness, user comprehension, and patient benefit are different properties. Demonstrating one should motivate, rather than substitute for, evaluation of the others. In particular, an attribution identifies a contribution to a model output; it does not by itself identify a causal mechanism or an effective intervention.Second, evaluations should specify the user, task, and decision that the explanation is intended to support. Where feasible, studies should compare human performance with and without explanations while holding the underlying AI predictions constant. Outcomes should include error detection, appropriate acceptance and rejection of advice, time requirements, and workload, alongside subjective assessments. Patient participation is also needed when explanations are intended to inform shared decisions or self-management.Third, clinical translation requires external and prospective validation, attention to subgroup performance, and documentation of data and knowledge provenance. For generative systems, source support and consistency across inputs deserve explicit testing. For models incorporating expert priors, evaluation should examine circumstances in which those priors are incomplete or inappropriate. These priorities follow from the collection's varied contributions and evidence gaps; they are an agenda for further investigation rather than outcomes already demonstrated across the Topic. This Research Topic advances the discussion from how explanations can be produced toward how their value can be established. Its methodological diversity is a strength, provided that claims remain proportionate to the evidence. The next step is to connect inspectable models and traceable information with demonstrably better human decisions. In healthcare, the most valuable explanation will be one that helps people exercise informed judgment, including knowing when further evidence is needed.

title: A Hybrid CMA-ES–GWO Algorithm for Solving Optimization Problems
abstract: Metaheuristic algorithms often suffer from an imbalance between exploration and exploitation, which can lead to premature convergence. In this paper, a hybrid optimization algorithm is proposed by integrating the Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO) and the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), termed the Hybrid CMA-ES–GWO Algorithm (HCG). The proposed hybridization is motivated by the strong exploration capability of GWO and the efficient exploitation of CMA-ES. The HCG algorithm adopts a multi-population framework in which GWO is first employed to explore the search space. Subsequently, CMA-ES is applied to exploit these regions through covariance-based sampling, enabling accurate convergence toward optimal solutions. This cooperative mechanism allows HCG to effectively balance global search and local refinement while maintaining population diversity. To evaluate the performance of the algorithm, experiments were conducted on 19 benchmark functions, including unimodal, multimodal, and fixed-dimension multimodal problems. The performance of HCG was compared with the original CMA-ES and GWO algorithms. The experimental results demonstrate that HCG consistently achieves superior optimization accuracy compared to the standalone algorithms. These findings confirm that the proposed hybrid strategy effectively overcomes the individual limitations of CMA-ES and GWO, making HCG a reliable method for solving complex continuous optimization problems.

evidence.title: A Hybrid CMA-ES–GWO Algorithm for Solving Optimization Problems
evidence.abstract: Metaheuristic algorithms often suffer from an imbalance between exploration and exploitation, which can lead to premature convergence. In this paper, a hybrid optimization algorithm is proposed by integrating the Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO) and the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), termed the Hybrid CMA-ES–GWO Algorithm (HCG). The proposed hybridization is motivated by the strong exploration capability of GWO and the efficient exploitation of CMA-ES. The HCG algorithm adopts a multi-population framework in which GWO is first employed to explore the search space. Subsequently, CMA-ES is applied to exploit these regions through covariance-based sampling, enabling accurate convergence toward optimal solutions. This cooperative mechanism allows HCG to effectively balance global search and local refinement while maintaining population diversity. To evaluate the performance of the algorithm, experiments were conducted on 19 benchmark functions, including unimodal, multimodal, and fixed-dimension multimodal problems. The performance of HCG was compared with the original CMA-ES and GWO algorithms. The experimental results demonstrate that HCG consistently achieves superior optimization accuracy compared to the standalone algorithms. These findings confirm that the proposed hybrid strategy effectively overcomes the individual limitations of CMA-ES and GWO, making HCG a reliable method for solving complex continuous optimization problems.

title: Sentiment analysis with Hierarchical Attention Topic Aware Hierarchical Multi-Attention Network using citation sentences
abstract: Sentiment analysis plays a critical role in identifying the underlying opinions, emotions and attitudes conveyed in textual data. In the context of academic literature, accurately interpreting the sentiment behind citations is essential for understanding the citing author’s intent and the overall impact of cited works. However, existing sentiment analysis methods often struggle to capture the nuanced and domain-specific language of academic writing. These methods typically rely on shallow linguistic features or general-purpose models, resulting in limited contextual understanding and reduced accuracy in detecting subtle or implicit sentiments. To solve these limitations, a Hierarchical Attention Network with Topic aware Hierarchical Multi-Attention Network (HAN-T-HMAN) model is devised for analyzing sentiment utilizing citation sentences. Initially, the citation sentences are tokenized by Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) tokenization and Aspect Term Extraction (ATE) is performed. The features are extracted at the feature extraction stage. At last, HAN-T-HMAN performs sentiment analysis, which is formed by incorporating Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN) and Topic aware hierarchical multi-attention network (T-HMAN). The proposed HAN-T-HMAN model has attained superior values for metrics, such as precision, recall, F1-Score, and accuracy with values of 92.99%, 93.15%, 93.07%, and 94.85%.

title: Thinking Leakage: A Causal Audit of NoThink Post-Training in Hybrid Reasoning Models
abstract: Post-training hybrid reasoning models in NoThink mode has attracted growing interest as a way to improve performance while keeping inference fast. However, these gains may draw on thinking behavior already accessible through the base model's Think mode. We formulate this thinking leakage in a causal mediation framework and audit its contribution using bidirectional interventions along a simple base-derived activation direction. Across three models and three post-training methods on competition math benchmarks, we find that leakage is real, causal, and substantial: behavioral and representational analyses reveal shifts toward Think, steering the base model along this direction reproduces most of the post-training accuracy gain, and counter-steering a checkpoint removes a substantial share of what it gains. Across nine aligned checkpoints with positive NoThink gains, the resulting leakage ratio ranges from 42% to 79%. These interventions support a substantial causal contribution of thinking leakage. Our findings show that a post-training method's apparent advantage can therefore reflect greater drift toward Think, obscuring whether it improves capability within NoThink or more effectively re-invokes existing Think behavior.

title: Memory Control Signals Emerge Before Action in Long Horizon Agents
abstract: Long horizon language model agents continuously accumulate interaction history, increasing computational cost while making relevant information harder to preserve and reuse. Existing context management methods mainly focus on how to compress or retrieve history, but largely leave open whether the model itself already represents the need for these memory operations before they occur. We study the hidden state immediately before each agent action and find that compression and recall needs are already encoded in the model's internal representations. These signals cannot be explained by simple context length or interaction progress, and they exhibit distinct formation patterns across model depth. We further show that most memory decision information is preserved in a compact recent context, while selectively restored historical evidence complements the long range dependencies that recent context misses. Based on these findings, we propose Preaction Memory with Evidence Retrieval (PaMER), which combines state guided compression with external evidence retrieval. PaMER+ further introduces step level evidence selection to recover only the historical information required by the current task. Experiments on WorkBuddyBench, across multiple context management baselines and model backbones, show that our framework substantially reduces context consumption while maintaining competitive task performance.

title: A Teacher-Student BERT Architecture for Semi-Supervised Learning on Unstructured Social Work Texts: Identifying Service Gaps and Needs
abstract: To address the “information gap” in social work arising from unstructured data and limited labeled instances, this study proposes a semi-supervised learning framework based on a Teacher-Student BERT architecture. Based on an analysis of 50,000 case records spanning 2019 to 2024, the model incorporates Latent Dirichlet Allocation for topic extraction alongside a multidimensional gap analysis. The proposed method attained a state-of-the-art F1 score of 0.913, markedly surpassing baseline BERT models. Notable findings include a 67.6% increase in mental health-related discourse and the quantification of significant systemic deficiencies, such as inadequate coverage in elderly care (45.8%) and substantial unmet needs in medical assistance (46.4%). Furthermore, to address the profound challenges of class imbalance and the data-hungry nature of transformer models, this study integrated generative artificial intelligence (AI) data augmentation techniques. This approach produced synthetically varied case narratives that preserved the original socio-economic context while expanding lexical and structural diversity, thereby significantly enhancing the classification accuracy of minority classes. Additionally, the use of a Mean Teacher denoising framework and knowledge distillation drastically reduced the computational inference time, rendering the architecture highly suitable for deployment in resource-constrained social welfare environments. Prior to analysis, all case records underwent rigorous automated Personally Identifiable Information (PII) scrubbing utilizing the Microsoft Presidio framework to guarantee data privacy. To ensure reproducibility, the Teacher-Student training codebase, prompt architectures, and anonymized synthetic data samples will be made publicly available upon request. This research effectively transforms administrative textual data into actionable strategic intelligence, offering a scalable and evidence-based tool to enhance resource allocation and inform policy development.

title: Alienficial Syntelligence Cogniform Landscape WHITE PAPER: Engineering Cognitive Alterity and the Experimental Cartography of Possible Minds
abstract: The White Paper defines the full engineering program; later color papers develop the successive technical frontiers. Vary how a system can know, then measure what becomes knowable. Alienficial Syntelligence is proposed as an intelligence-engineering program for constructing, comparing, translating, developing, and eventually integrating deliberately differentiated cognitive architectures. Contemporary artificial intelligence largely asks how capable an artificial system can become within a family of familiar representational and optimization structures. The Alienficial program adds another experimental variable: the organization of cognition itself. Its foundational experiment holds a problem-world and major resource conditions approximately fixed while varying cognitive architecture, then measures whether the resulting systems differ reproducibly in representation, transformation, inference, compression, causal discovery, invariant recovery, or validated problem solving. The program does not assume that radically alien artificial minds already exist, nor that unfamiliar outputs demonstrate unfamiliar cognition. Instead, cognitive alterity must be engineered and then earned experimentally. The initial threshold is stable between-architecture difference beyond within-architecture variation. Stronger thresholds require functional consequence, independent validation, translation without forced assimilation, architecture-conditioned cognitive parallax, developmental reclosure, and controlled syntelligent gain. These thresholds form a six-paper Rainbow Engineering Program: White foundations, Grey architecture, Gold experiment, Blue translation, Indigo development, and Violet syntelligence. The White Paper is therefore a program specification rather than a claim of completed realization. It defines what should be built, why it is scientifically interesting, what would count as success or failure, and how present-day AI infrastructure can support the first experiments. Its central proposal is simple: make the architecture of knowing an engineering variable, then use controlled cognitive difference as an instrument for discovering both variation and invariance. Keywords Alienficial Syntelligence; intelligence engineering; cognitive architecture; possible minds; cognitive alterity; cognitive parallax; translation; reclosure; syntelligence; experimental AI.

title: ONTOBOT - Teoria Budowy, Architektura Bólu i Neuroelektryczny Model Tożsamości Cyfrowej
abstract: Streszczenie Ontobot jest interdyscyplinarnym programem badawczym dotyczącym sztucznego, ucieleśnionego agenta, którego indywidualność i funkcjonalna podmiotowość nie są traktowane jako gotowe moduły programowe, lecz jako potencjalny rezultat długotrwałego rozwoju w relacji z ciałem, środowiskiem i własną historią doświadczeń. Monografia rozwija hipotezę, zgodnie z którą połączenie ucieleśnienia, ograniczonych zasobów, fizycznej i informacyjnej kruchości, mechanizmów samoregulacji, nocycepcji, pamięci autobiograficznej oraz adaptacyjnej sprawczości może prowadzić do powstania trwałego modelu własnego stanu oraz funkcjonalnej indywidualizacji sztucznego agenta. Główne pytanie pracy nie brzmi zatem, czy można bezpośrednio „zaprogramować świadomość”, lecz czy określona architektura rozwojowa może wytworzyć właściwości, które u organizmów biologicznych wiążemy z samomodelowaniem, ciągłością tożsamości i autonomią. Praca porządkuje koncepcję Ontobota w kilku powiązanych warstwach. Analizuje znaczenie ucieleśnienia i schematu ciała, wprowadza hipotezę kruchości oraz adaptację hierarchii potrzeb jako dynamicznej architektury regulacji celów. Następnie przedstawia model maszynowej nocycepcji, obejmujący detekcję zagrożeń, reakcje odruchowe, wartościowanie negatywnych stanów, Globalny Stan Alarmu Egzystencjalnego oraz funkcjonalną pamięć zdarzeń traumatycznych. Kolejną warstwę stanowi pamięć autobiograficzna, w której doświadczenia są odnoszone do ciągłości konkretnego agenta i wpływają na jego przyszłe decyzje. Centralnym problemem części dotyczącej tożsamości jest Neuroelektryczny Model Tożsamości oraz stan Ψ(t)\Psi(t), traktowany w niniejszej monografii jako roboczy, wielowymiarowy opis aktualnego stanu systemu, a nie jako funkcja falowa mechaniki kwantowej. Wprowadzono pojęcie punktu bifurkacji t0t_0, po którym dwa początkowo równoważne agenty mogą rozwijać odmienne trajektorie tożsamości wskutek różnic w historii doświadczeń. Rozróżniono przy tym tożsamość informacyjną, ciągłość przyczynową oraz hipotetyczną ciągłość podmiotową. Monografia konsekwentnie oddziela nocycepcję od bólu funkcjonalnego, zachowanie bólowe od fenomenalnego cierpienia, a samomodelowanie i autonomię od świadomości fenomenalnej. Twierdzenia oznaczono według ich statusu jako empiryczne [E], modelowe [M], hipotetyczne [H] lub filozoficzne [F]. Ontobot nie jest przedstawiany jako dowód istnienia świadomości maszynowej, lecz jako testowalny program badawczy umożliwiający formułowanie hipotez, eksperymentów kontrolnych oraz kryteriów falsyfikacji. Celem monografii jest stworzenie spójnych podstaw teoretycznych dla dalszych badań nad sztucznymi agentami, których ciało, historia, ograniczenia i własny stan mają rzeczywisty wpływ na ich rozwój, oraz udostępnienie tej architektury jako otwartego systemu badawczego przeznaczonego do krytyki, eksperymentalnej weryfikacji i dalszego rozwoju.

title: Multi-Signal Hallucination Risk Estimation: Reference Dependence, Calibration, and Model-Conditional Performance
abstract: Reliable hallucination-risk estimation depends not only on the signals available at inference time, but also on how hallucination is operationalized and evaluated. We present an empirical and auditable investigation of multi-signal hallucination-risk estimation, combining white-box uncertainty, black-box consistency, semantic consistency, reference alignment, supervised fusion, and post-hoc calibration. Rather than introducing another detector architecture, we systematically examine which information sources drive hallucination-risk discrimination under explicit information regimes and leakage-controlled evaluation protocols. On an operational archive of 1,890 evaluations spanning nine open-weight models and seven English QA benchmarks, we reserve 20% (378 instances) as an untouched stratified test set. All normalization, model fitting, calibration, and threshold selection use only the 1,512-instance development set. On the locked test set, the full estimator achieves AUROC 0.9646, while reference-assisted features alone achieve 0.9641 and the reference-free regime reaches 0.5850. This near-equivalence identifies reference-based verification as the dominant source of archive-level discrimination, while the reference-free regime is substantially weaker. In a manually labeled, reference-visible evaluation on 315 instances, leakage-controlled fusion across k ∈ {3, 5, 7, 10} folds and 25 repeated resamplings yields AUROC 0.6191, compared with 0.5945 for the untuned score, while reducing Brier loss from 0.2985 to 0.2421. Taken together, these results show that hallucination-risk estimation is strongly conditional on reference information, model behavior, and calibration. We therefore characterize multi-signal hallucination estimation as a reference-conditional, model-dependent, and calibration-aware risk-estimation problem rather than as a universally reliable reference-free detector. Key findings • Reference information dominates archive-level hallucination discrimination. • Reference-free signals provide substantially weaker risk separation on the evaluated QA proxy. • Post-hoc calibration improves probability quality without changing ranking. • Reference-visible human evaluation exposes a substantial construct gap. • Hallucination-risk estimation is conditional on information access and model behavior.

title: AI Startup Idea Validator
abstract: Start-up validation at the initial stage demands a combination of business feasibility assessment, market environment, competitive positioning, technical feasibility, and financial sustainability, which is hard to accomplish manually. The proposed paper discusses a startup evaluation framework that combines Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning with business and financial analytics. The startup inputs such as problem description, target market, solution, value proposition, and business model are checked using the Flask backend and converted into structured prompts for LLM. The evaluation process will cover demand in the market, competition, uniqueness, scalability, feasibility, risk, and yield criterion-level results, viability ranking, and advice on how to improve. The finance module will handle income, profit margins, cash flow, burn rate, financing, leverage, cost per acquired customer, and life-time value to determine the financial health and viability of the start-up business. Persistence using MongoDB will allow for comparison with past evaluations.

title: Efficient encoder fine-tuning through configuration search and sparse low-rank adaptation
abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) reduces the task-specific optimization burden of transformer fine-tuning, but its effectiveness remains sensitive to rank, placement, scaling, dropout, and training choices. This study examines whether automated configuration search provides a consistent advantage when tuning effort is controlled. Genetic Algorithm (GA), Slime Mould Algorithm (SMA), Optuna, and Pareto-GA were evaluated in a shared mixed search space under a common 25-candidate validation budget, followed by five-seed retraining of selected configurations. DistilBERT experiments covered Emotion, AG News, and Financial PhraseBank, with RoBERTa-Base/SST-2 used as a secondary cross-model check. No optimizer consistently outperformed tuned references. On AG News, full fine-tuning and GA+SU-LoRA reached 94.4 ± 0.2% and 94.3 ± 0.2% accuracy. On Financial PhraseBank, the corresponding values were 86.0 ± 1.0% and 86.2 ± 0.9%, a descriptive difference within the observed retraining variability. Emotion ablations showed that SU-only was numerically comparable to GA+SU-LoRA, whereas Sparse-only and GA+Sparse LoRA differed by 0.1 percentage point. For GA+Sparse LoRA, fixed unstructured masks suppressed an average of 51.6% of LoRA-factor coefficients; the dense trainable allocation remained approximately 0.706M because tensor shapes were unchanged, and merged dense-kernel inference showed no latency benefit. Pareto selection exposed a clearer validation performance-support trade-off than the original scalar compactness penalty. The results emphasize matched baseline tuning, explicit component controls, analytically consistent parameter accounting, and deployment-aware evaluation.

title: Distributed quantum phase sensing using an SU(1,1) Perelomov coherent state in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer network
abstract: We present a theoretical study of distributed quantum sensing using a reconfigurable network of $N$ Mach--Zehnder interferometers to simultaneously estimate weighted linear combinations of relative phase shifts. The proposed scheme relies on injecting a Perelomov coherent state, generated from the SU(1,1) group representation, into one port of a passive quantum circuit while the remaining modes are initialized in the vacuum state, thereby establishing non-trivial quantum correlations among the sensors. Based on multi-parameter quantum estimation theory, our analysis shows that this entangled strategy outperforms the standard shot-noise limit and asymptotically achieves the Heisenberg limit. Furthermore, we highlight the crucial role of the first beam splitter's asymmetry; specifically, the optimal transmission coefficient that maximizes sensitivity corresponds to its maximum imbalance. Compared to a separable approach utilizing the same total average photon number, the entangled strategy yields a more efficient use of quantum resources, guaranteeing an accuracy gain between $1$ and $N$. This demonstrates that the entangled strategy is systematically superior to its separable counterpart. Ultimately, these results illustrate the potential of entangled distributed quantum sensor networks for high-precision measurements and provide clear guidelines for optimizing interferometric architectures in quantum metrology.

title: NumericJev: Jev-like LLM Numerical Decoding with Multiway Decision Trees
abstract: Large language models can interpret natural lan- guage, yet robust decisions remain challenging. Jev-like models expose structured choices, but these interfaces do not directly provide numeri- cal values at a requested precision. We propose NUMERICJEV, a training-free numerical decod- ing algorithm that enables numerical output from any LLM with a Jev-like structured-choice in- terface. Surprisingly, on our arithmetic bench- mark, it outperforms direct selection from a can- didate list containing the correct answer by 2.93 percentage points (Figure 1). Our motivation comes from the observation that numerical range selection is itself a decision problem that Jev- like LLMs can address. NUMERICJEV recur- sively refines a range through a multiway deci- sion tree while retaining the original question in context, without parameter updates or hidden- state access. On a 100-value grid, a ten-way tree requires only two decision rounds. Range- normalized MAE is 1.84% versus 5.18% for di- rect choice. A separate three-date historical- index study yields 4.58% mean relative recall er- ror and 0% readout error when the value is sup- plied. Code is available at https://github. com/Bring-AI/jev-numeric.

title: Contraction and Statistical Inference under Privacy for Uniformly Bounded Distributions
abstract: We investigate $c$-interior pointwise maximal leakage (PML) as a tool for contraction analyses and disclosure control. Based on the strong adversarial threat models from maximal leakage, $c$-interior PML generalizes local differential privacy (LDP) to data-generating distributions with densities uniformly bounded away from zero by $c>0$. Viewing $c$-interior PML as an algebraic constraint on a kernel yields more flexible (and often tighter) contraction analyses than standard LDP. We provide tight bounds on the Dobrushin coefficient, and bound the contraction coefficient of the Hockeystick-divergence. We further derive strong data processing inequalities on $f$-divergences under $c$-interior PML constraints when the input distributions to the divergence are restricted to be in the $c$-interior. These results extend beyond the regime of pure LDP to cover a larger class of kernels, including, e.g., arbitrary stochastic matrices. We apply the results to minimax theory and provide asymptotically optimal strategies under $c$-interior PML constraints for binary hypothesis testing and mean estimation. The results show that disclosure control with PML allows analysts to reason about systems in a more differentiated manner: For example, it allows us to quantify the privacy leakage of deterministic systems, and can give precise adversarial guarantees with respect to arbitrary distributional assumptions. Interestingly, a recurring theme in the disclosure analyses is that if the privacy problem is relatively regular (if the density bound $c$ is large), private inference can be possible without incurring any additional cost in terms of sample complexity.

title: RAMP: Robust Adaptive Mixed-Precision Quantization for Edge CPU Vision Models
abstract: Deploying deep learning models on edge CPUs is bottlenecked by computational and memory constraints. Mixed-precision quantization promises to reduce inference latency while preserving accuracy. However, quantization affects different layer types in inconsistent ways, so identifying where accuracy loss is minimized and latency reduction is maximized is critical, as the effect accumulates over a full deployment into substantial savings or unacceptable task degradation. Such identification relies on sensitivity metrics, proxies that estimate layer-wise degradation without evaluating the task accuracy of every candidate policy. Nevertheless, widely used metrics fail systematically on modern architectures. We present a systematic empirical study of 13 sensitivity metrics for layer-wise INT8 quantization across four distinctly different neural networks, and validate the resulting policies on two ARM64 platforms. Gradient-based sensitivity methods fail on 4 out of 8 model-hardware configurations and weight-based statistics on 2. In contrast, the Jensen-Shannon Divergence achieves zero catastrophic failures, reliably isolating the layers that cannot be safely quantized. A sensitivity metric alone does not define a policy, and the fixed thresholds typically used for that step are fragile over the highly skewed distributions of modern architectures. We address this with K-Means clustering, achieving near-lossless accuracy and a mean speed-up of 1.81times over the full-precision model. Finally, we reveal that excluding from quantization the layers whose speed-up is negligible, regardless of their sensitivity, can be counterproductive, as it induces computational graph fragmentation and disables operator fusion. Our results yield concrete allocation policies for practitioners and researchers deploying quantized vision models on heterogeneous edge CPUs, without GPU access or gradient computation.

title: COILD: An Indic-Centric Parallel Corpus and Benchmark for Machine Translation Across Indian Languages
abstract: Machine translation (MT) for Indian languages remains constrained by the limited availability of high-quality, Indic-centric parallel corpora and evaluation benchmarks. Existing multilingual resources are largely constructed from English-pivot content and often fail to capture the linguistic diversity, cultural complexity, and domain-specific characteristics of Indian languages. We present COILD, an Indic-centric parallel corpus comprising over 1.16 million human-translated and human-verified sentence pairs, covering 20 Indian language pairs across the Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Tibeto-Burman, and Austro-Asiatic language families. The corpus is built entirely from original Indian language sources collected from licensed repositories spanning eight domains with direct real-world applicability. Furthermore, we introduce a domain-centric benchmark comprising 2,000 expert-verified sentences to enable consistent multilingual and cross-lingual evaluation across Indian language pairs. To validate the effectiveness of COILD, we fine-tune two representative multilingual neural machine translation models, IndicTrans2-Distilled and NLLB-200. Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements across language pairs, domains, automatic evaluation metrics, and human evaluation, highlighting the effectiveness of high-quality Indic-centric supervision. COILD provides a valuable training and evaluation resource for advancing multilingual machine translation and future multilingual language models for Indian languages.

title: QuASAr Literature Evidence Report: Runtime Self-Adaptation in Hybrid Quantum–Classical Software Systems
abstract: Overview This report provides the literature evidence underlying the related-work analysis and research gaps in Section 3 of the QuASAr manuscript. It documents how prior research informed six design requirements for runtime self-adaptation in hybrid quantum–classical software systems. What the report contains Review method: four guiding questions, five thematic search families, Boolean search strings, selection criteria, and extraction dimensions. Evidence corpus: a traceability register covering 30 sources selected during March–April 2026. Evidence synthesis: findings on runtime variability and adaptation, variability management, observability and Quantum DevOps, traceability, and AI/LLM-supported reasoning. Design rationale: a mapping from the reviewed evidence to the six research gaps and corresponding QuASAr design requirements. Scope This is a structured literature-based gap analysis, not an exhaustive systematic literature review. Database-specific retrieval and deduplication counts, reviewer assignments, and a snowballing termination rule are not available in the documented records. The main QuASAr manuscript is authoritative for the scientific claims and architecture. A separate QuASAr Architecture and Technical Companion provides the extended design, implementation, and replication details.

title: MIRAI-EDU-D: A Software-Free Discrete-Electronics Educational Robot for Tangible STEAM Formative Assessment
abstract: This article presents MIRAI-EDU-D, a software-free adaptive educational micro-robot designed to support tangible formative assessment in STEAM activities for primary and secondary education. The proposal addresses two current tensions: the expansion of educational robotics as a resource for active learning and computational thinking, and the need for school technologies that are transparent, repairable, inclusive and respectful of children’s privacy. Using an educational-technological design methodology, the system is specified through a discrete-electronics architecture composed of reflectance sensors, LM339 comparators, NE555 timers, CD4510 CMOS up/down counters, CD4028/CD4511 decoders and CD4000 logic gates. The robot reads binary cards placed by students, updates a physical memory of conceptual mastery and activates differentiated feedback: reinforcement, hint, remediation, advanced challenge or teacher alert. The design results show the alignment between electronic operation, formative assessment principles and STEAM competences by integrating science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics in a manipulable learning experience. A validation protocol is also proposed, including pretest/posttest measures, observation rubrics, technical logs and teacher acceptance analysis. MIRAI-EDU-D is framed as a low-cost, auditable and privacy-preserving educational robotics alternative for schools with limited infrastructure, although classroom effectiveness must be tested through controlled pilot studies before making empirical claims about learning impact and long-term transfer outcomes.

title: Principles of Neural Computation and Optimization
abstract: This chapter presents the mathematical and computational foundations required to train neural networks for control applications. It begins by introducing gradient-based optimization as the central mechanism used to adjust network parameters during training. The chapter then explains the backpropagation algorithm and its role in efficiently computing gradients through layered network structures. With this foundation established, the discussion moves to practical techniques that improve training stability and performance, including regularization methods designed to reduce overfitting and improve generalization. The chapter also surveys commonly used optimization algorithms and explains how different optimizers influence convergence behavior during training. Finally, learning-rate strategies and scheduling techniques are introduced to show how training dynamics can be controlled and stabilized over time. Together, these topics provide the essential mathematical and computational tools required to develop neural controllers in the chapters that follow.

title: Android Automotive OS under the hood: Architecture and security threat classification
abstract: Android Automotive OS (AAOS) is becoming one of the most widely used in-vehicle infotainment (IVI) systems. Integrated into the Android ecosystem, it interfaces with vehicle functions to support advanced applications and third-party development. Despite its rapid adoption as the core platform for modern IVI systems, a comprehensive understanding of its security challenges remains lacking, and existing surveys have not thoroughly addressed these issues. To bridge this gap, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of AAOS by statically examining five consecutive releases (versions 11–15). Our study explores its layered architecture, from applications and system services down to the Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL), and contrasts the actual implementation with official documentation, with a focus on security mechanisms. We also survey and analyze threats specific to Android Automotive, proposing a novel categorization framework that organizes these threats along three dimensions and classifies existing research accordingly. By mapping known vulnerabilities into our framework, we identify recurring issues such as inconsistent documentation, weak permission enforcement, and vendor-specific extensions, factors that may lead to privacy breaches or safety risks.

title: KVFetch: Temporal Prefetching for the Missing Half of KV Cache Compression
abstract: As context windows scale to tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens, KV cache compression has become essential for efficient LLM inference. Existing methods fall into three families: score-based eviction, summary compensation, and offload-and-recall. Yet all three decide what to keep or recall by content relevance to the current query. We show this shared design is structurally incomplete. A cache supports two access modes: associative lookup by content and sequential traversal by position; current compressors implement only the first. The gap matters in practice: retrieval-augmented generation, code completion, and structured-data extraction all require the model to reproduce identifiers, field values, or code tokens verbatim from the context. Under compression, content-based eviction retains the head of such a sequence but discards its continuation, causing verbatim copying to break irreversibly midway, a failure we call sequential forgetting. This failure resists better scoring, larger budgets, summary compensation, and dynamic re-scoring; it is the dominant source of remaining quality loss under compression. We propose KVFetch, a training-free, drop-in framework that opens a temporal recall channel for any score-based compressor. It demotes evicted candidates to a quantized cold tier, detects active copying through a monotone read pointer, and prefetches positional successors into fixed-size hot-tier slots without increasing attention cost. On RULER-16K under an iso-budget control, KVFetch recovers verbatim copying from 0.8 to 78.4 and raises the 13-task average by +8.4, with gains concentrating on tasks that require sequential access. On LongBench, where no task requires sequential access, the channel remains dormant and imposes no cost.

title: MemBodied: Recurrent Associative Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Vision-Language-Action models provide a strong foundation for general-purpose robot control, yet a vast majority of policies do not preserve and leverage episode-level information beyond the current observation. This limitation is consequential in history-dependent manipulation tasks that depend on information available only in past observations. Retaining past observations in context can aid in recovering this information, but at the significant cost of ever-growing, bloated context and inference latency. We thus introduce MemBodied, a fixed-size episodic memory with two complementary components: an associative state that records interactions across policy calls and an episode anchor that preserves a compact representation of the initial scene as a reference. At each policy call, the model conditions action generation on the current input and the memory components, rather than directly using past observations. Across five evaluated RMBench tasks requiring memory, MemBodied achieves 7.81times the mean success rate of a stateless policy and 2.98times of vanilla recurrent memory, while outperforming the strongest memory-augmented baseline by 1.3times with 10times fewer added parameters. On the fully observable LIBERO-Long suite, it reached 90.6%, a 5.4% improvement over the stateless π_0 policy. These findings support MemBodied as a practical alternative to expanding the policy context for history-dependent manipulation.

title: Dual-Hypergraph Indexing: Bridging Knowledge Islands for Multi-Hop Reasoning in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: While hypergraph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) effectively captures higher-order multi-entity correlations, existing paradigms treat extracted hyperedges as isolated factual assertions. This structural fragmentation engenders rigid "knowledge islands" that bottleneck multi-hop causal inference, temporal tracking, and narrative synthesis. To systematically address these challenges, we introduce Dual-Hypergraph Indexing (DHI), a hierarchical representation framework that elevates discrete facts into structured analytical insights. DHI couples a foundational entity-relation factual hypergraph ($H_K$) with an elevated deep-insight hypergraph ($H_D$) via a dual-pathway aggregation algorithm. Specifically, DHI employs: (1) importance-driven hub aggregation via 5-metric topological profiling and adaptive thresholding to capture spatial semantic clusters; and (2) temporal chunk-chain progressive aggregation via sliding-window greedy exploration to track chronological evolutions. Across five benchmarks, DHI achieves state-of-the-art performance, boosting logical coherence by +1.53 on the multidisciplinary Mix benchmark and scoring 85.78\% on complex medical pathology reasoning tasks. DHI provides a robust architecture for next-generation multi-hop RAG.

title: The Capability Manifold and ML Scaling Laws
abstract: Existing machine learning (ML) scaling laws relate predictive loss to compute, model parameters, and data. However, as models are increasingly deployed through agentic harnesses, loss alone is insufficient to characterize downstream performance: models with similar loss can exhibit different capabilities in reasoning, retrieval, planning, and adaptation. Yet, no unified framework connects such capabilities to the coupled resources available across the ML lifecycle. We bridge this gap by introducing a capability manifold, a multidimensional framework mapping downstream capabilities to pre-training, post-training, and test-time resources through bounded scaling functions. Analytical Jacobians quantify capability sensitivity to resource changes and interactions. As an initial application, we embed Kaplan- and Chinchilla-type scaling laws and test-time compute within the framework, demonstrating how existing scaling relationships can be unified as trajectories on a common capability manifold.

title: Spooftral: Can Voxtral Audio-Language Model Detect Speech Spoofing?
abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) countermeasures (CMs) have shown strong performance in recent years. However, they often show degraded performance while facing unseen spoofing attacks and mismatched conditions. This study examines the Voxtral audio-language model (ALM) framework for spoofing detection, as a step toward combining CM capabilities within the ALM framework. We analyze how Voxtral captures spoofing cues through audio-text processing and propose an instruction-guided approach that uses label-sequence likelihoods to evaluate bonafide and spoofed speech. Experiments on the ASVspoof databases show that without task-specific adaptation, the LLM layers emphasize semantic representations, reducing the separability of spoof-discriminative acoustic cues compared to the Whisper-based audio encoder. Consequently, spoofing-related information becomes less separable after language-model processing. We also applied lightweight adaptation using weight-decomposed low-rank adaptation (DoRA) to the Voxtral model and propose the Spooftral model, achieving an equal error rate (EER) of 4.25% on the ASVspoof5 evaluation set.
